title: What do I love (10.6)
hookLine: not bodily beauty, yet a kind of light, voice, fragrance, food, embrace
tomorrow: after you've asked the sky, where do you look for God?

lines: WHAT DO I LOVE, WHEN I LOVE YOU?
cards: Scroll back through a good week on a phone: a sunset, a meal, someone laughing, a song played on repeat. Book ten of the Confessions opens with a question that sorts through a list like that.
Augustine has told his past, and his mother is buried; now he writes in the present tense. He says his love for God isn't in doubt. The question is stranger than whether.
In his Latin: Quid autem amo, cum te amo? But what do I love, when I love you?

teach.b: First, the no. Not the beauty of bodies, he says, not light that pleases the eyes, not sweet songs, not the scent of flowers, not manna and honey, not arms made for embracing. Second, the yes, and it's a surprise.
In his Latin: et tamen amo quandam lucem et quandam vocem et quendam odorem et quendam cibum et quendam amplexum.

teach.h: AND YET, A KIND OF LIGHT.
teach.b: And yet I love a kind of light, a kind of voice, a kind of fragrance, a kind of food, a kind of embrace.
The same five senses come right back, each with a kind of in front: a light no place can hold, a taste that eating doesn't use up. Third, the asking. So he asks creation.
The earth says, I am not he.
The sea, the winds, the sky, the sun, the moon and the stars answer: we are not your God; seek above us. Then all together: he made us. Fourth, how they answer.
His question, Augustine says, was his looking at them, and their answer was their beauty.
The world isn't God's rival here. It's a witness, pointing past itself.

how: Catholics are taught that creation's beauty reflects God who made it, and the Catechism quotes Augustine, from one of his sermons, on questioning the beauty of the earth, sea and sky as a way from the world to God.

games.q: what does “what do i love” mean?
o: the light, voice and embrace behind all beauty
nothing at all that the senses can reach

s: Augustine says loving God means not caring about beautiful things
he loves 'a kind of light, a kind of voice'; the senses come back, pointing further.
in book ten, creation answers Augustine: we are not your God
seek above us, they say, and then together: he made us.
Augustine wasn't sure whether he loved God at all
he says his love is certain. the question is what he loves.

games.q: your little sister asks if loving her dog means she loves God less. what fits Augustine's book ten?
o: loving what's beautiful can point you to the one who made it.
yes; loving God means giving up the things you love here.
no, because the dog and God are really the same thing.
games.why: Augustine asks creation, and it answers: we are not your God; he made us. Their beauty is a witness, not a rival.

practice: Find something you can smell or taste right now: coffee, an orange peel, bread, the air at an open window. Take it in slowly, and let it be both itself and a pointer, the way Augustine's sea and stars pointed past themselves.
If you pray, you can ask his question once: what do I love, when I love you?

wordCard.voice: What do I love. Augustine's question in book ten, answered with a kind of light, voice, fragrance, food and embrace.
